Halloween is a shortened Scottish phrase about saints.

The word Halloween began as a Scottish shortening of All Hallows even, meaning the evening before All Hallows, or All Saints Day. Hallow is an old word for a holy person or saint, and the short form is recorded from the 1560s.

Halloween means the evening before the saints' day.

Autumn yellow was hiding in the leaf all summer.

Chlorophyll gives leaves their green color and powers photosynthesis through the growing season. As nights lengthen in autumn, chlorophyll production slows and the pigment is destroyed. That unmasks the yellow and orange carotenoids and red anthocyanins in the leaf.

Fall color is what remains when the green fades.

Werewolf comes from late Old English werewulf, joining wer, meaning man, with wulf, meaning wolf. The word grew rare after the 1600s and was broadly revived in the early 1800s through folklore studies.

A werewolf is, word for word, a man wolf.

The most enjoyable scare sits in the middle.

Aarhus University researchers fitted 110 visitors to a haunted attraction in Denmark with heart rate monitors. Enjoyment peaked at a moderate level of fear and dropped when people were barely scared or too scared. Research suggests fear feels good when it moves the body just far enough from its normal state, much like play.

Fear turns into fun inside a narrow window.

Candy corn began in the 1880s, later sold as Chicken Feed.

Candy corn was invented in the 1880s by George Renninger, who worked for the Wunderle Candy Company. In 1898 the Goelitz Confectionery Company, now Jelly Belly, bought the recipe and sold it as Chicken Feed, a nod to the country's farming roots. Each colored layer was once poured by hand into a kernel shaped mold.

A seasonal sweet began as a tribute to farm life.

An owl's wing feathers are shaped to erase sound.

Owl flight feathers carry comb-like serrations on their leading edge that break up the turbulent air behind a wing's usual swoosh. A velvety feather surface and a soft fringe on the trailing edge dampen what is left. Together they streamline the airflow and absorb the sound of flight.

Silence is built into the shape of the feather.

Mischief Night first shows up in writing at Oxford, 1790.

The earliest known use of the term Mischief Night comes from Oxford in 1790. It then meant the night before May Day, when young people switched shop signs and overturned water tubs. Parts of New England now call the night before Halloween Cabbage Night, and Detroit calls it Devil's Night.

The urge to prank has simply moved around the calendar.

Haunt entered English in the early 1200s from Old French hanter, to frequent or visit regularly, and in Middle English to haunte scole meant to attend school. The ghostly sense of a spirit returning to the house where it had lived appears in Shakespeare, in A Midsummer Night's Dream around 1590.

A ghost haunts a house the way a regular haunts a cafe.

A Minnesota town answered Halloween pranks with a parade.

After years of soaped windows, tipped outhouses and cows loose on Main Street, civic leaders in Anoka, Minnesota, proposed a large Halloween celebration in 1920. That first year brought a parade, a bonfire at Bridge Square, and bags of popcorn, candy and peanuts for the children. The town has held it every year since, except 1942 and 1943 during World War II.

A town chose to give its restless kids something to belong to.

The pumpkin's family was farmed in Mexico 10,000 years ago.

Botanically, a pumpkin is a fruit, because anything that starts from a single flower is classed as a simple fruit. Seeds and rind of Cucurbita pepo, the species most carving pumpkins belong to, were found in Guila Naquitz cave in Oaxaca, Mexico. Researchers dated that cultivation to between 10,000 and 8,000 years ago, earlier than maize or beans.

The porch pumpkin comes from one of the oldest farmed plants in the Americas.

Most faces we see in objects read as male.

Seeing faces in outlets, clouds or carved pumpkins is called face pareidolia. In a 2022 study of 3,815 adults, people readily gave these illusory faces an emotion, an age and a gender. 90% of the images had an average rating of male, and only 9% female.

The brain assigns a whole personality to a pattern.

Your goosebumps are built for fur you no longer have.

Goosebumps may help animals with thick fur stay warm, but humans do not seem to benefit much from the reaction. Harvard researchers found in mice that the cells behind goosebumps also help regulate the stem cells that regrow hair. Research suggests the reflex stayed because it quietly does a second job.

A leftover reflex that still has work to do.

A bonfire was once, quite literally, a bone fire.

Bonfire appears in English in the late 1300s as bonfir or banefire, meaning a fire in which bones are burned. That original sense faded and was forgotten by the 1700s. By the mid 1500s the word already meant a large open air fire for celebration.

The word began as bone plus fire.

Before candy, there were soul cakes at the door.

Soul cakes were small spiced cakes, often marked with a cross of dried fruit or a cut in the top. Poorer neighbors went to the doors of wealthier households around All Hallows, singing and performing, and were given the cakes. Britannica notes that trick or treat is thought to have come from this British custom of letting the poor beg for soul cakes.

Asking at the door began as a way of feeding the poor.

Day of the Dead grew from Mesoamerican and Catholic roots.

The Day of the Dead comes from the traditions of Indigenous peoples of Mesoamerica, including the Aztecs, Toltecs, Olmecs and Maya, who saw death as a continuation of life. It blends those rituals with All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day, which Spanish colonizers introduced.

Death is treated as a continuation, not an ending.

A French abbot gave the dead their own day.

The November 2 day of prayer for all the dead is credited to Odilo, abbot of Cluny in France, who died in 1048. The date was chosen to follow All Saints' Day, and by the end of the 13th century it was observed almost everywhere in the Western church.

Remembering the dead became a shared act instead of a private grief.
